screens.title: What is Packaging?
screens.narratorSegment: Packaging is the process that takes your project's source code, assets and configuration, compiles them when necessary, and produces a standalone application that players can run. In Unreal terms, that means the editor gathers your. uasset and. umap files, compiles C++ code into platform-specific binaries, includes selected content and plugins, and writes out an executable or app bundle and accompanying data. The goal is to produce a self-contained build targeted for a platform, with only the runtime parts required to run the game. A clear concrete example: when you package for Windows 64-bit, the editor creates an executable and folders containing cooked assets specially formatted for runtime on Windows. A common misconception is that packaging simply copies project folders; it does more — it cooks and compiles assets, strips editor-only code, and applies the chosen build configuration optimizations. Packaging matters because a poorly configured package will miss maps, crash at startup, or include editor-only debugging capabilities. The key takeaway: know what your packaging tool includes and verify maps and plugins before starting a full package pass. Which asset or setting would you double-check before packaging your project?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › What is Packaging?
Packaging — formal definition

Packaging converts your project into a platform-ready, distributable build by cooking assets, compiling code and bundling configuration into an executable and data folders.

Analogy
Think of packaging as creating a travel-ready suitcase: you pack only what is needed at runtime, and leave editor-only items and tools behind.
Common misconception
Packaging is not a straight file copy. It transforms and optimizes assets and code to run efficiently on the target platform.
Key Takeaway

Packaging makes a distributable game by cooking assets and compiling code for the chosen platform. Verify settings and maps before packaging.

What is included in a package?
  • C++ compiled binaries for the target platform.
  • Cooked asset data (.uasset in runtime form) and packaged maps.
  • Selected plugins and runtime configuration files.
  • Platform-specific resources and startup executable.
Example scenario
You set Default Maps in Project Settings, choose Windows 64-bit, select Shipping, and produce a folder containing an .exe and cooked content. Running that exe verifies your packaged game.

screens.title: DebugGame, Development, and Shipping
screens.narratorSegment: Build configurations change how your project is compiled and what runtime behavior is included. DebugGame includes full debugging symbols and runtime checks, making it the slowest but ideal when you need to step through code or inspect memory. Development removes some heavy debug-only behaviors and enables profiling hooks, producing a faster build that still helps internal testers and developers profile problems. Shipping strips debugging symbols, logging and editor-only code to produce the smallest, fastest executable intended for public release. A concrete example: a Development build might include extra logging that helps your QA team reproduce a crash, but a Shipping build removes those logs and the developer console so players cannot access debug commands and your executable runs with maximum optimizations. A common misconception is to assume Development and Shipping only affect file size; they change available features and runtime diagnostics as well. When packaging choose Shipping for final releases and Development when you need profiling, while reserving DebugGame for deep engine or logic debugging. The key takeaway is to match your build configuration to the goal: debug, test, or distribute. Which configuration will you use for your next test run and why?

keyIdea.title: Build choices matter
keyIdea.text: DebugGame for deep debugging, Development for testing and profiling, Shipping for optimized public releases.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Build Configurations
DebugGame
Includes full debugging symbols and checks. Best for stepping through engine or gameplay code when you need deep insight.
Development
Optimized for testing with some debugging and profiling hooks retained. Good for internal QA and performance checks.
Shipping
Strips debugging and editor features. Smallest, fastest build intended for public release and final distribution.
Practical comparison
Use this short checklist before packaging: do you need logging and the developer console? If yes, prefer Development; if releasing to users, choose Shipping. DebugGame is for step-by-step troubleshooting only.
Example
A QA build using Development includes profiling markers so you can measure frame time; the Shipping build used for release will remove those markers to reduce overhead.
Common mistake
Packaging a public release as Development leads to larger files and exposed debug features. Always confirm the build configuration before packaging a release.
Key Takeaway

Match build configuration to your objective: debug, test, or ship. Incorrect selection leads to performance issues or leaked debug features.

screens.title: Packaging: Editor steps and automation
screens.narratorSegment: Packaging can be started from the Unreal Editor using the File → Package Project menu or run via command-line tools as part of automated builds. From the editor, choose the target platform such as Windows (64-bit), select the destination folder, and pick your build configuration. Before you click package, confirm Project Settings: default maps, game instance, and any required plugins must be enabled. Automation is useful for continuous integration: command-line packaging avoids manual menu clicks and ensures repeatable builds. The chapter notes that command-line tools are more robust for automated builds; while specific commands are platform- and engine-version-dependent, the principle is consistent: script the packaging steps, set environment variables for platform and configuration, and ensure the build machine has required SDKs and plugins installed. A concrete example: set up a CI job that checks out the repository, ensures DerivedDataCache is not committed, runs a scripted package step for Windows Shipping, and stores the produced build artifact for testing. A common misconception is that automation requires the Editor GUI; in fact, headless packaging via the engine build tools is standard for repeatable release pipelines. The takeaway: use the Editor for one-off builds and command-line automation for reliable, repeatable CI packaging.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Packaging Steps & Automation
Manual Editor steps
  1. Open Project and confirm Default Maps in Project Settings.
  2. File → Package Project → choose Platform (e.g., Windows → Windows (64-bit)).
  3. Select destination folder, choose build configuration, then start packaging.
  4. After completion, run the produced executable to verify correct startup and content.
Checklist before packaging
  • Default maps set and saved.
  • Plugins enabled and configured for the platform.
  • Packaging settings review for included/excluded content.
Automation notes
Automate packaging using engine build tools or command-line packaging in CI. Automation ensures repeatable builds and integrates with testing pipelines. Ensure the CI runner has required SDKs and that DerivedDataCache is not tracked in Git.
CI example (conceptual)
A CI job checks out code, restores dependencies, runs a scripted package step for Shipping Windows, and uploads the build artifact for QA to download.
Key Takeaway

Use the Editor for manual verification but automate packaging for repeatability and CI-driven releases.

screens.title: Project settings, plugins, and what to check before packaging
screens.narratorSegment: Before packaging, confirm several project-level settings and plugin states that are required for runtime. The most critical checks include Default Maps in Project Settings — if no map is set, the packaged game may not open the intended level by default. Ensure the Game Instance and related startup classes are configured so your save and session logic initializes correctly at runtime. Verify that any plugins your project depends on are enabled and set to be included in the package; missing plugin binaries will break the packaged executable. Also review Packaging settings to include or exclude content folders intentionally and to configure additional assets for cook-on-the-fly scenarios. A concrete example: if your main menu is a plugin-provided UI and the plugin is disabled, the packaged build may skip loading the menu and crash. A common misconception is assuming editor-only plugins are harmless to leave enabled; some editor-only assets can be excluded, but runtime plugins must be included. Finally, test the packaged build on the target platform — local verification avoids shipping builds that fail immediately for users. The takeaway: perform a pre-package checklist of maps, game instance, and plugins, and run the packaged exe before release. What plugin or setting will you verify first in your project?

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Project Setup
Essential settings
  • Default Maps (Project Settings → Maps & Modes).
  • Game Instance and startup classes configured.
  • Required plugins enabled and set to package with builds.
  • Packaging settings reviewed for included/excluded folders.
Example failure
When a plugin that provides the main menu is disabled or missing from the package, the packaged game may fail to initialize UI and crash at startup.
Pre-package checklist
Save maps, verify default map entries, enable required plugins and set them to be packaged, and ensure packaging settings include essential content. Then run a test package and execute the produced binary to confirm behavior on the target platform.
Pro tip
Close the editor before performing Git operations to avoid locked files and false positives in git status.
Key Takeaway

A short pre-package checklist prevents common runtime failures: maps, game instance, plugins, packaging settings, and a quick run of the built exe.

screens.title: Packaging and Git mistakes to avoid
screens.narratorSegment: There are a few recurring mistakes that cause the most trouble when packaging and using Git with Unreal projects. First, packaging a public release as Development rather than Shipping results in unnecessarily large files, possible exposed debug features, and slower runtime. Second, committing generated folders such as Binaries, Intermediate, and DerivedDataCache will bloat your repository, slow clones, and produce constant merge conflicts. A concrete example: if a teammate commits Binaries, every other clone will fetch large platform-specific binaries that are unnecessary and often cause conflicts across OSes. Third, forgetting to enable plugins or default maps produces packaged builds that crash at startup — these are often diagnosed only after players report issues. On the Git side, a common misconception is that. gitignore is optional; it is essential for Unreal projects due to the volume of generated files. Another mistake is infrequent commits: large, monolithic commits make it hard to revert changes and to review code. The remedy is simple: always use a focused. gitignore, commit small logical changes frequently, and verify build configuration before packaging. The closing question: what is the worst outcome if you ship a Development build to players, and how would you prevent it?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Mistakes to avoid
Packaging mistakes
  • Shipping vs Development confusion: Shipping removes debug features; Development keeps profiling hooks.
  • Forgetting to include necessary plugins or default maps.
  • Not testing the packaged executable before release.
Git mistakes
  • Committing Binaries, Intermediate or DerivedDataCache and bloating the repo.
  • No .gitignore or an overly permissive one that still tracks generated files.
  • Large, infrequent commits that are hard to review and revert.
Real example
A repo with Binaries committed can quickly reach gigabytes, slowing clones and causing merge conflicts when different developers build different platform binaries.
Key Takeaway

Prevent problems by using a proper .gitignore, selecting the correct build configuration, and testing packaged builds before distribution.

screens.title: Core Git commands for Unreal projects
screens.narratorSegment: Git provides the safety net every team needs. The basic workflow is concise: stage changes, commit them with a clear message, push to a remote, and pull updates from teammates. The most common commands you'll run are git add to stage changes, git commit with a descriptive message to record them locally, git push origin branch-name to upload commits to a remote, and git pull origin branch-name to synchronize changes from others. A concrete example: after closing the editor, you might run git add. to stage your code and config changes, then git commit -m "Add main menu and audio setup" to save a logical unit of work. A common misconception is that git add. blindly commits everything you care about; in Unreal projects you must ensure. gitignore prevents large generated files from being staged. Another frequent mistake is pushing without pulling first — always pull before starting new work to reduce merge conflicts. The takeaway: commit frequently with small logical changes, use clear messages, and keep your local branch synchronized with the remote. Which commit message style will you adopt for clarity in your team?

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Git Basics
Commands you'll use
git add .
git commit -m "Your descriptive message"
git push origin <branch-name>
git pull origin <branch-name>
Stage, save locally, push to remote, and pull updates. Replace <branch-name> with your active branch such as main or develop.
Best practices
  • Commit frequently with small, logical changes.
  • Pull before you start new work to minimize conflicts.
  • Use clear commit messages explaining what changed and why.
Example workflow
Close the editor, run git status to review, stage intended files, commit with a clear message, then push to your remote branch.

screens.title: Why .gitignore matters and what to exclude
screens.narratorSegment: . gitignore tells Git which files and folders to ignore so the repository tracks only the files you want. For Unreal Engine projects this is essential because the engine generates large binary and cache folders that change frequently. The chapter lists common exclusions such as Binaries, Build, DerivedDataCache, Intermediate and Saved. Also exclude IDE-specific files like. vs and. idea and temporary or log files. Committing these generated files will bloat your repository size, slow down clones, and create merge conflicts because generated files differ per machine and platform. A concrete example: if DerivedDataCache is committed, every developer will download large cache blobs that are machine-specific and unnecessary; this increases clone time and disk usage. The recommended approach is to create a. gitignore in the project root containing these exclusions and to initialize Git only after confirming the ignore file is correct. A common misconception is to include everything to guarantee a build; instead, track only source (. cpp,. h), essential assets (. uasset,. umap) and configuration (. ini). The takeaway: a correct. gitignore protects collaborators and keeps the repo usable.

Intermediate/
Saved/
*.log
*.pdb
*.sdf
.DS_Store
This minimal list prevents the most common generated files from being tracked while keeping source and assets under version control.
Why these entries matter
  • Binaries and Build contain platform-specific compiled output that should not be versioned.
  • DerivedDataCache and Intermediate are generated caches that change frequently.
  • Saved contains logs and autosaves that are local to a developer environment.
Key Takeaway

A focused .gitignore keeps your repository small, reduces conflicts, and makes collaboration practical for Unreal projects.

screens.title: Git workflow for solo and team projects
screens.narratorSegment: For both solo and team workflows, some Git practices reduce friction and protect history. Commit often with small, logical units of work so you can revert specific changes if needed. For team projects use a branching strategy: keep main (or master) as the stable release branch, use develop for ongoing integration, and create feature branches for individual tasks. For solo projects a single main branch may suffice, but you should still commit frequently and tag release points. Always pull before starting new work and before pushing to avoid unnecessary merge conflicts. A concrete example: a developer creates feature/ui-fix, implements changes, commits frequently with messages like "Fix main menu layout and audio hook", pulls the latest develop to merge recent changes, resolves any conflicts locally, then pushes the feature branch and opens a merge request. A common misconception is that branches are expensive; in Git they are lightweight and intended for isolation. The takeaway: use clear branch names, pull before you push, and prefer small commits to large monolithic ones. Which branch naming convention will you follow in your team? Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Workflow & Branching
Branching patterns
  • main: stable release branch.
  • develop: integration branch for ongoing work.
  • feature/*: isolated branches for tasks and changes.
Practical rules
  • Pull before you start new work and before pushing changes.
  • Commit small logical changes with descriptive messages.
  • Use feature branches and merge via pull/merge requests for review.
Example
Create feature/level-load, commit incremental fixes, pull develop, resolve conflicts locally, push feature and open a merge request for integration.
Key Takeaway

Use branches to contain work, commit often, and keep your local branch synchronized by pulling before starting new tasks and before pushing.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn how to take a working Unreal project and turn it into a distributable build, and how to manage that project's history safely with Git. Packaging bundles your code, assets, and settings into a standalone executable targeted for a platform such as Windows or Mac. You'll also learn the practical differences between build configurations — DebugGame for deep debugging, Development for testing, and Shipping for public releases — and why using the right configuration matters for performance and size. On the version control side, we'll show how to initialize a repository, create a focused. gitignore that prevents binaries and generated caches from being tracked, and use simple Git operations like add, commit, push and pull to collaborate and back up your work. Throughout the chapter you'll run a small hands-on exercise: package a simple project for Windows, then initialize Git and verify that your. gitignore keeps large and temporary files out of the repo. By the end you will understand packaging choices, avoid common packaging mistakes, and have a safe Git workflow you can use on team projects. Consider right now: what would break first in your project if you published a Development build instead of Shipping?

These learning objectives focus your practice. First, you will understand the packaging pipeline: what gets compiled and what must be included in Project Settings to produce a working build. I will show why default maps and enabled plugins matter and how missing configuration causes runtime issues. Second, you will be able to produce a packaged build for a target platform, including selecting the build configuration suited to your goal — whether debugging, internal testing, or public release. Third, you'll configure a. gitignore tailored for Unreal Engine so your Git repository tracks only code, essential assets, and configuration while excluding temporary and derived files that bloat history. Finally, you'll perform essential Git operations: initialize a repository, stage and commit changes, push to a remote, and pull updates safely. Each objective is practical and tied to a concrete check: verify Project Settings, run a Packaging pass, open your. gitignore to ensure Binaries and DerivedDataCache are ignored, and run git status after your first commit. These are skills you will use every time you prepare a build or collaborate with others. Which check will you add first in your workflow?

This second objectives screen focuses on practical checks you can perform to prove you've learned the material. You should be able to verify Project Settings such as default maps and the game instance, and ensure necessary plugins are enabled before packaging. You will demonstrate packaging by producing a Windows (64-bit) build and launching the resulting executable to confirm maps and UI load correctly. On the version control side, you'll create a. gitignore that excludes Binaries, Intermediate, DerivedDataCache and Saved folders, then initialize Git and run git status to confirm large generated files are not tracked. You should also practice staging and committing small, logical changes frequently, and pulling before beginning new work to reduce merge conflicts. Finally, you'll be able to explain why Shipping builds are appropriate for release, and why committing generated binaries harms collaboration. These checks align directly with the lab tasks and will be used to verify your competency in packaging and safe Git usage. Which verification will you run first in your project?

Packaging is the process that takes your project's source code, assets and configuration, compiles them when necessary, and produces a standalone application that players can run. In Unreal terms, that means the editor gathers your. uasset and. umap files, compiles C++ code into platform-specific binaries, includes selected content and plugins, and writes out an executable or app bundle and accompanying data. The goal is to produce a self-contained build targeted for a platform, with only the runtime parts required to run the game. A clear concrete example: when you package for Windows 64-bit, the editor creates an executable and folders containing cooked assets specially formatted for runtime on Windows. A common misconception is that packaging simply copies project folders; it does more — it cooks and compiles assets, strips editor-only code, and applies the chosen build configuration optimizations. Packaging matters because a poorly configured package will miss maps, crash at startup, or include editor-only debugging capabilities. The key takeaway: know what your packaging tool includes and verify maps and plugins before starting a full package pass. Which asset or setting would you double-check before packaging your project?

Build configurations change how your project is compiled and what runtime behavior is included. DebugGame includes full debugging symbols and runtime checks, making it the slowest but ideal when you need to step through code or inspect memory. Development removes some heavy debug-only behaviors and enables profiling hooks, producing a faster build that still helps internal testers and developers profile problems. Shipping strips debugging symbols, logging and editor-only code to produce the smallest, fastest executable intended for public release. A concrete example: a Development build might include extra logging that helps your QA team reproduce a crash, but a Shipping build removes those logs and the developer console so players cannot access debug commands and your executable runs with maximum optimizations. A common misconception is to assume Development and Shipping only affect file size; they change available features and runtime diagnostics as well. When packaging choose Shipping for final releases and Development when you need profiling, while reserving DebugGame for deep engine or logic debugging. The key takeaway is to match your build configuration to the goal: debug, test, or distribute. Which configuration will you use for your next test run and why?

Packaging can be started from the Unreal Editor using the File → Package Project menu or run via command-line tools as part of automated builds. From the editor, choose the target platform such as Windows (64-bit), select the destination folder, and pick your build configuration. Before you click package, confirm Project Settings: default maps, game instance, and any required plugins must be enabled. Automation is useful for continuous integration: command-line packaging avoids manual menu clicks and ensures repeatable builds. The chapter notes that command-line tools are more robust for automated builds; while specific commands are platform- and engine-version-dependent, the principle is consistent: script the packaging steps, set environment variables for platform and configuration, and ensure the build machine has required SDKs and plugins installed. A concrete example: set up a CI job that checks out the repository, ensures DerivedDataCache is not committed, runs a scripted package step for Windows Shipping, and stores the produced build artifact for testing. A common misconception is that automation requires the Editor GUI; in fact, headless packaging via the engine build tools is standard for repeatable release pipelines. The takeaway: use the Editor for one-off builds and command-line automation for reliable, repeatable CI packaging.

Before packaging, confirm several project-level settings and plugin states that are required for runtime. The most critical checks include Default Maps in Project Settings — if no map is set, the packaged game may not open the intended level by default. Ensure the Game Instance and related startup classes are configured so your save and session logic initializes correctly at runtime. Verify that any plugins your project depends on are enabled and set to be included in the package; missing plugin binaries will break the packaged executable. Also review Packaging settings to include or exclude content folders intentionally and to configure additional assets for cook-on-the-fly scenarios. A concrete example: if your main menu is a plugin-provided UI and the plugin is disabled, the packaged build may skip loading the menu and crash. A common misconception is assuming editor-only plugins are harmless to leave enabled; some editor-only assets can be excluded, but runtime plugins must be included. Finally, test the packaged build on the target platform — local verification avoids shipping builds that fail immediately for users. The takeaway: perform a pre-package checklist of maps, game instance, and plugins, and run the packaged exe before release. What plugin or setting will you verify first in your project?

There are a few recurring mistakes that cause the most trouble when packaging and using Git with Unreal projects. First, packaging a public release as Development rather than Shipping results in unnecessarily large files, possible exposed debug features, and slower runtime. Second, committing generated folders such as Binaries, Intermediate, and DerivedDataCache will bloat your repository, slow clones, and produce constant merge conflicts. A concrete example: if a teammate commits Binaries, every other clone will fetch large platform-specific binaries that are unnecessary and often cause conflicts across OSes. Third, forgetting to enable plugins or default maps produces packaged builds that crash at startup — these are often diagnosed only after players report issues. On the Git side, a common misconception is that. gitignore is optional; it is essential for Unreal projects due to the volume of generated files. Another mistake is infrequent commits: large, monolithic commits make it hard to revert changes and to review code. The remedy is simple: always use a focused. gitignore, commit small logical changes frequently, and verify build configuration before packaging. The closing question: what is the worst outcome if you ship a Development build to players, and how would you prevent it?

Git provides the safety net every team needs. The basic workflow is concise: stage changes, commit them with a clear message, push to a remote, and pull updates from teammates. The most common commands you'll run are git add to stage changes, git commit with a descriptive message to record them locally, git push origin branch-name to upload commits to a remote, and git pull origin branch-name to synchronize changes from others. A concrete example: after closing the editor, you might run git add. to stage your code and config changes, then git commit -m "Add main menu and audio setup" to save a logical unit of work. A common misconception is that git add. blindly commits everything you care about; in Unreal projects you must ensure. gitignore prevents large generated files from being staged. Another frequent mistake is pushing without pulling first — always pull before starting new work to reduce merge conflicts. The takeaway: commit frequently with small logical changes, use clear messages, and keep your local branch synchronized with the remote. Which commit message style will you adopt for clarity in your team?

. gitignore tells Git which files and folders to ignore so the repository tracks only the files you want. For Unreal Engine projects this is essential because the engine generates large binary and cache folders that change frequently. The chapter lists common exclusions such as Binaries, Build, DerivedDataCache, Intermediate and Saved. Also exclude IDE-specific files like. vs and. idea and temporary or log files. Committing these generated files will bloat your repository size, slow down clones, and create merge conflicts because generated files differ per machine and platform. A concrete example: if DerivedDataCache is committed, every developer will download large cache blobs that are machine-specific and unnecessary; this increases clone time and disk usage. The recommended approach is to create a. gitignore in the project root containing these exclusions and to initialize Git only after confirming the ignore file is correct. A common misconception is to include everything to guarantee a build; instead, track only source (. cpp,. h), essential assets (. uasset,. umap) and configuration (. ini). The takeaway: a correct. gitignore protects collaborators and keeps the repo usable.
